translations.title: All Systems Go
translations.explanation: A linear system can be represented compactly by a matrix equation A x=b. Each row of the coefficient matrix A holds the coefficients from one equation, and the variable column x must use the same variable order throughout. An augmented matrix [A|b] records the system for elimination. Elementary row operations produce an equivalent system: exchange rows, multiply a row by a nonzero constant, or replace a row by itself plus a multiple of another row. Row reduction distinguishes a unique solution from infinitely many solutions and inconsistent systems. When A is square and invertible, the solution is x=A⁻¹b; if A is singular there is no such inverse and row reduction must be interpreted directly. In the original All Systems Go painting-supplies context, three purchase totals provide three equations for the unknown unit prices of paint, brushes, and masking tape. A correct 3×3 coefficient matrix records zero wherever an item was not bought, and the inverse solution must be interpreted as prices rather than just an ordered triple. In the actual MVP 10.6H student sequence, the painting receipts first reappear from the earlier 10.1H activity. Students then multiply 3×3 matrices to recognize the identity and inverse laws, construct AX=B for the receipts, multiply by A⁻¹, and finally apply the same method to a different three-equation system. The method requires recording the inverse obtained with technology, not just an unexplained numerical triple.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For x+y+z=6, 2x−y+z=3, x+2y−z=2, the matrix equation is [[1,1,1],[2,−1,1],[1,2,−1]]·[x,y,z]ᵀ=[6,3,2]ᵀ. Legal row operations are Ri↔Rj; Ri←kRi with k≠0; and Ri←Ri+kRj. A row [0,0,0|c] with c≠0 means inconsistency; a zero row with free variables may indicate multiple solutions. For invertible square A, multiplying Ax=b by A⁻¹ yields x=A⁻¹b. Matrix multiplication order matters: A⁻¹b, not bA⁻¹. For an invertible 2×2 matrix A=[[a,b],[c,d]], det(A)=ad−bc must be nonzero and A⁻¹=(1/(ad−bc))[[d,−b],[−c,a]]. Check dimensions before multiplying A⁻¹b; a 2×2 inverse cannot multiply a 3-entry constants vector.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — solve a 3×3 system: form [1 1 1|6; 2 −1 1|3; 1 2 −1|2]. Apply R₂←R₂−2R₁ to obtain [0 −3 −1|−9]; apply R₃←R₃−R₁ to obtain [0 1 −2|−4]. Then R₂←R₂+3R₃ gives [0 0 −7|−21], so z=3. Back-substitute y−2(3)=−4 to get y=2 and x+2+3=6 to get x=1. Verify in all three original equations: 6, 3, and 2. Example 2 — inconsistent system: x+y=2 and 2x+2y=5 produce a row [0,0|1] after subtracting twice row 1; no solution exists. Example 3 — compute an inverse, then solve: 2x+y=5 and x+y=3 give A=[[2,1],[1,1]], b=[5,3]ᵀ and det(A)=2·1−1·1=1. Thus A⁻¹=[[1,−1],[−1,2]] and A⁻¹b=[5−3,−5+6]ᵀ=[2,1]ᵀ. Check: 2(2)+1=5 and 2+1=3. Example 4 — technology for 3×3: return to Example 1 and enter the ordered coefficient matrix A and column b into a matrix-capable tool. Check det(A)=7, so A is invertible. The verified inverse is A⁻¹=(1/7)[[−1,3,2],[3,−2,1],[5,−1,−3]]. Compute A⁻¹b=(1/7)[−6+9+4,18−6+2,30−3−6]ᵀ=[1,2,3]ᵀ. Confirm AA⁻¹=I and Ax=b; if the tool produces decimals, test the original equations instead of treating rounded entries as exact. Example 5 — singular does not always mean inconsistent: x+y=2, 2x+2y=4 has infinitely many solutions (x=2−t,y=t); replacing 4 with 5 gives no solutions. Both coefficient matrices have determinant zero and no inverse. Example 6 — painting-supplies context, adapted from the MVP student task: let p be dollars per gallon of paint, q dollars per brush, and r dollars per roll of masking tape. Three shopping totals give 2p+r=30, p+4q=20, and 2q+r=10. In variable order [p,q,r]ᵀ, A=[[2,0,1],[1,4,0],[0,2,1]], c=[30,20,10]ᵀ, so A[p,q,r]ᵀ=c. The zeros correspond to supplies absent from each purchase. det(A)=10, so A is invertible. A⁻¹=(1/10)[[4,2,−4],[−1,2,1],[2,−4,8]], which yields [p,q,r]ᵀ=[12,2,6]ᵀ. Therefore paint costs $12 per gallon, a brush costs $2, and masking tape costs $6 per roll. Check all original totals: 2(12)+6=30, 12+4(2)=20, and 2(2)+6=10. Counterexample to careless contextual acceptance: if only the third total were $50, the same invertible matrix would produce [−4,6,38]ᵀ. That triple satisfies the altered equations but a negative paint price is not plausible; discuss the data instead of calling it an inconsistent linear system. Example 7 — source-goal matrix properties and second system, first-party walkthrough: with the painting coefficient matrix P=[[2,0,1],[1,4,0],[0,2,1]], I₃P=P and P⁻¹P=I₃ (also PP⁻¹=I₃). The source gives a decimal-form candidate inverse P⁻¹=[[0.4,0.2,−0.4],[−0.1,0.2,0.1],[0.2,−0.4,0.8]], equivalent to the exact fractional inverse in Example 6. Check a complete product gives I₃ before using P⁻¹ on [30,20,10]ᵀ. For the additional 10.6H application x+2y+2z=16, 2x+y+3z=17, x+2y+z=13, form C=[[1,2,2],[2,1,3],[1,2,1]] and d=[16,17,13]ᵀ. det(C)=3; its checked inverse is C⁻¹=(1/3)[[−5,2,4],[1,−1,1],[3,0,−3]], so C⁻¹d=[2,4,3]ᵀ. Confirm: 2+2(4)+2(3)=16, 2(2)+4+3(3)=17, and 2+2(4)+3=13. Technology can supply the inverse, but students should still verify CC⁻¹=I₃, carry the correct variable order and show each matrix step.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Choose and label the variable order; transcribe all coefficient signs correctly into A and constants into b. 2. Write [A|b] and select a nonzero pivot (swap rows if needed). 3. Use legal operations to eliminate entries under successive pivots. 4. Continue to echelon or reduced echelon form and interpret zero rows before claiming uniqueness. 5. Back-substitute or read variable values from reduced echelon form. 6. Substitute the proposed values in EVERY original equation. 7. If using A⁻¹b instead, independently verify that A is square/invertible and that Ax=b. 8. To use the inverse method on a 2×2 system, calculate ad−bc first. If it is nonzero, form A⁻¹ with the correct signs and 1/determinant factor, multiply A⁻¹b in that order, and check Ax=b. 9. For dimension 3×3 or larger, use appropriate matrix technology to find a candidate inverse, inspect determinant/rank, calculate A⁻¹b and independently check both AA⁻¹=I and every original equation. If A is singular, do not attempt A⁻¹; row-reduce [A|b] to distinguish dependent from contradictory equations. 10. Compare substitution/elimination, row reduction, and inverse methods: they should agree on an invertible system, but only row reduction can classify all singular cases. 11. For the painting-supplies task, name the price variables and lock the order [paint, brush, tape]. Translate the three receipts into equations, then A=[[2,0,1],[1,4,0],[0,2,1]] and c=[30,20,10]ᵀ. Evaluate det(A)=10, use a verified 3×3 inverse or a trusted matrix tool to calculate A⁻¹c, and check all three receipts before interpreting the unit prices. 12. Treat missing items as zero coefficients; do not swap the brush and tape columns without changing the variable vector too. For a different set of totals, a negative unit price can be algebraically valid but contextually impossible; report that modeling limitation separately from matrix singularity. 13. Follow the six-part 10.6H progression: demonstrate I₃P=P and P⁻¹P=I₃; identify the identity/inverse properties; write the paint receipts as PX=b; compute X=P⁻¹b and interpret all three unit prices; then apply the same inverse-matrix argument to the separate 3×3 source system Cx=d, showing the inverse and checking all equations. 14. For the additional 3×3 example, use the full coefficient order [x,y,z], determinant 3, numerator inverse [[−5,2,4],[1,−1,1],[3,0,−3]] and exact answer [2,4,3]; reject a row/column swap and any answer that satisfies only one equation.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not reorder variables between equations or lose negative signs in the augmented matrix. Multiplying a row by zero destroys equivalence. A row such as [0,0|1] signifies a contradiction, not a new variable. Not every square matrix is invertible. Do not confuse matrix multiplication with componentwise multiplication, and do not compute bA⁻¹ where dimensions or order are wrong. Always check solutions in the original system. A zero determinant means no inverse; it does not by itself mean that the equations have no solutions. For a computed inverse, verify multiplication gives the identity before using it. Matrix software output may be rounded, so numerical agreement alone is not proof of exact equality. In the source painting-supplies model, the first receipt has zero brushes, the second has zero tape, and the third has zero gallons of paint; inserting a nonzero coefficient for an unpurchased item changes the data. An invertible system can also give negative prices for altered receipts: this is an invalid real-world interpretation, not proof of an algebraic contradiction. The All Systems Go source task is not just the earlier shopping problem: it asks for identity and inverse matrix products before the model and then a second 3×3 system. An answer giving only the prices without showing A⁻¹A=I and the additional solved system misses that reasoning progression. Inverse entries shown as decimals must still be checked to avoid rounding or sign mistakes.
translations.quickSummary: Represent a linear system as Ax=b and [A|b], reduce rows using equivalence-preserving operations, classify solution count and check in the original equations. Use x=A⁻¹b only when A is invertible.

translations.title: Log Logic
translations.explanation: A logarithm answers an exponent question. For a base b>0 with b≠1, y=log_b(x) means exactly bʸ=x, so exponential and logarithmic functions are inverses. Logarithms are defined only for x>0 in the real number system. Their graphs reflect exponential graphs across y=x: the exponential curve passes through (0,1), while its inverse logarithm passes through (1,0). The logarithm is increasing when b>1 and decreasing when 0<b<1. Use a logarithm when a variable is in the exponent, and check the domain before accepting a solution. In the source Log Logic activity, put known and estimated logarithms on a number line and justify each position from exponential powers. Not every comparison between logarithms with different bases has one fixed direction for every positive argument.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Inverse identity: log_b(bˣ)=x for real x, and b^(log_b x)=x for x>0; b>0 and b≠1. log_b 1=0, log_b b=1. A logarithmic function has domain x>0, range all real numbers, and vertical asymptote x=0. For b>1 it grows; for 0<b<1 it decreases. log_b(xy)=log_b x+log_b y applies only for x,y>0; log_b(x+y) generally does NOT split into a sum. Change of base: log_b x=ln(x)/ln(b) for x>0 and valid b. For b>1, logarithms preserve order: 0<x<y implies log_b x<log_b y. For 0<b<1, they reverse order: 0<x<y implies log_b x>log_b y. The quotient rule log_b(x/y)=log_b x−log_b y requires x>0 and y>0. The power law log_b(x^r)=r log_b x is valid for x>0 and real r. These are not licenses to take logs of zero or negative real numbers.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: log₂(32)=5 because 2⁵=32. Example 2: log₃(1/9)=−2 because 3⁻²=1/9. Example 3: solve log₂(x)=−3. Rewrite 2⁻³=x, so x=1/8; checking log₂(1/8)=−3 verifies it. Example 4: solve 2ˣ=7. The inverse gives x=log₂ 7=ln 7/ln 2≈2.807; substituting gives approximately 7. Graph the matching points (3,8) on y=2ˣ and (8,3) on y=log₂ x, which are reflections over y=x. Example 5 — reason about logs without a calculator: because 2<3<4 and b=2>1, 1=log₂2<log₂3<log₂4=2. For a base between zero and one, ordering reverses: 3<5 implies log_(1/2)(3)>log_(1/2)(5), and both values are negative because (1/2)⁰=1 and the arguments exceed 1. Example 6 — compare logs in different bases: log₄3=ln3/ln4=(1/2)log₂3, so 0<log₄3<log₂3. Example 7 — justify the product rule: let u=log_b x and v=log_b y for positive x,y. Then b^(u+v)=b^u·b^v=xy, so log_b(xy)=u+v. The same reasoning does not give log_b(x+y)=u+v: log₂(6)≠log₂(2)+log₂(4)=3. Example 8 — apply the domain before solving: log₂(x−3)=1 requires x>3, and exponentiating gives x−3=2, hence x=5, which satisfies the domain and the original equation. Example 9 — number-line reasoning without a logarithm button: for base 3, log₃(1/9)=−2, log₃(1/3)=−1, log₃1=0, log₃3=1, and log₃9=2, in that left-to-right order. The exponents give the exact locations; to locate log₃5, use 3<5<9 so 1<log₃5<2. Example 10 — test a claimed universal comparison of bases: log₂(x)<log₃(x) is NOT true for every x>0. At x=1 both are 0; for x>1, ln(x)>0 and ln(2)<ln(3), so log₂(x)>log₃(x); for 0<x<1, ln(x)<0 and the inequality reverses to log₂(x)<log₃(x). The argument must be positive. Check using exact powers: log₂9>3>log₃9=2, but log₂(1/9)<−3<log₃(1/9)=−2. A single observed example cannot prove a statement about every positive x.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the base b and verify b>0, b≠1. 2. Convert log_b(x)=y into bʸ=x, or convert bʸ=x into log_b(x)=y. 3. Solve the equivalent equation using known powers or the change-of-base formula as appropriate. 4. Check that every logarithm input is strictly positive; discard extraneous answers. 5. If interpreting a graph, exchange input/output coordinates across the line y=x and label the logarithmic vertical asymptote. 6. Check your answer by evaluating the corresponding exponential form. 7. When comparing two logarithms with the same valid base, first ensure both arguments are positive and then use increasing order for b>1 or reversed order for 0<b<1; bound unknown values between powers of the base. 8. To compare different bases, use a valid change-of-base expression or equivalent powers. 9. To justify log laws, translate them to products or quotients of positive exponential expressions; never distribute logarithms across addition. 10. For an open-ended claim, state the domain and write an explicit inverse-exponent or monotonicity argument rather than presenting a decimal alone. 11. To position logarithms on a number line, first evaluate inverse powers exactly (including zero and negative exponents), then bound unknown entries between nearby known powers of their positive valid base; explain placements without relying solely on decimals. 12. Before accepting a conjecture comparing log₂x and log₃x for all x>0, split the domain into 0<x<1, x=1, and x>1; the sign of ln(x) changes, so a claimed universal strict inequality fails.
translations.commonMistakes: log_b(x) is an exponent, not b×x or x/b. Negative LOGARITHM VALUES are permitted, but logarithm inputs must be positive. Bases cannot equal 0, 1, or a negative real number in this context. The false rule log_b(x+y)=log_b x+log_b y must not be used. Inverse notation does not mean taking a reciprocal. An exponential has a horizontal asymptote; its logarithmic inverse has a vertical one. Comparing logarithms without checking whether 0<b<1 reverses order can invert the correct inequality. Do not use log_b(x/y) for invalid nonpositive inputs, and do not mistake a justified ordering task for a single exact-number response. A logarithm comparison observed at x>1 cannot be generalized unchanged to 0<x<1; both expressions equal zero at x=1. Placing logarithms on a number line without explaining inverse-power bounds omits the source task's reasoning goal.
translations.quickSummary: log_b x=y ↔ bʸ=x for b>0, b≠1 and x>0. Exponential and logarithmic graphs reflect across y=x. Use inverse operations to solve exponent equations and check the logarithm's positive input.
